extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for forming, testing, and accepting scientific hypotheses and for resolving observed laws into more general laws by deduction and induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction from verified premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductions must be from premises established by legitimate canons of experimental inquiry, and the results must be tested by verification by specific experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Deductive Method is to predominate only when its premises have been legitimately established experimentally. Anti-pattern: deducing from 'premises hastily snatched up, or arbitrarily assumed' (the Baconian error). Example: Newton's inverse-square law began as an hypothesis but became acceptable because it led deductively to Kepler's laws and was verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by specific experience
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis which serves to explain facts must be submitted to the canons of legitimate induction and actually tested by specific experience to be entitled to be received as truth rather than as a mere technical aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing means deriving consequences and checking them against observation/experiment. Scoring note: a hypothesis untested by induction remains provisional no matter how explanatory it appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution into more general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer explanations that resolve observed special uniformities (derivative laws) into simpler and more general laws (ultimate or more general antecedents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good scientific progress often consists in showing that many special empirical generalizations are consequences of simpler laws (e.g., atomic theory explaining chemical proportions; electricity explaining magnetic phenomena). Anti-pattern: treating every empirical rule as final when it may be derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Use methods of experimental contrast (Method of Difference) to establish necessity or causal roles — e.g., proving the necessity of water for putrefaction by showing dry preserved flesh does not putrefy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit experimental contrasts that isolate the factor of interest provide strong inductive evidence. Example cited: dryness preventing putrefaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for all cases meeting law conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new law is discovered, examine all cases that present the conditions necessary for bringing that law into action to find further demonstrations and explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the law to diverse contexts where its antecedent conditions exist (e.g., Faraday's law: wherever a conductor moves at right angles to a magnet expect electrical evolution). Use such searches both to confirm and to extend the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive concrete consequences across contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: From a general law deduce particular consequences in multiple domains and check whether they accord with observation (e.g., permeability of gases through membranes implies explanations for absorption of environmental gases, spread of CO2 from effervescent drinks, alcohol vapour absorption, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong explanatory law yields many specific, testable consequences; enumerate and test them. Scoring: breadth and accuracy of deduced consequences strengthen the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain via intermediate links (causal chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide deductive chains of intermediate processes that connect cause to observed effect (e.g., tartaric+bicarbonate → tartrate → conversion to carbonate requires oxygen → abstraction of oxygen reduces assimilation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good explanations identify proximate causes and intermediate chemical/physical steps. Anti-pattern: stopping at an empirical correlation without attempting to show mechanistic intermediates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility by analogy to known laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses gain plausibility when they 'ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature' rather than being wholly fanciful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that posit agents or laws analogous to established phenomena. Anti-pattern: inventing both a fictitious agent and a fictitious law with no analogue in known science (purely arbitrary hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two legitimate forms of hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize two kinds of hypotheses: (1) the agent is real but the law of its operation is supposed, and (2) the agent is fictitious but supposed to act according to laws similar to known phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Newton's inverse-square began as (1); Descartes' vortices were (2). Use this taxonomy to assess how speculative a hypothesis is and what kinds of evidence would support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis as a tool to deduce known and new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition made (without sufficient evidence) to deduce conclusions in accordance with facts known to be real; its purpose is to explain by deduction and to lead to testable consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate hypotheses by whether they successfully deduce already-known facts and predict new ones. Anti-pattern: hypotheses that explain nothing beyond restating phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of chimerical universal reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid claims that all phenomena can be explained by a single cause without rigorous justification; such totalizing reductions are often chimerical unless grounded in demonstrable links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical caution: attempts to reduce all phenomena to one cause have often been premature. But attempting reduction is legitimate if based on evidence and can be tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits: ultimate vs derivative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish derivative laws (deducible from more general ones) from ultimate laws (which cannot be further resolved); ultimate laws correspond at least in number to distinguishable qualities of sensations or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that some elements of explanation will always remain as laws of particular kinds (e.g., a law of color) even after discovering antecedents; do not confuse reduction of modes of production with elimination of the law-type itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of unitary antecedent for each distinguishable phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ideal limit' of explanation is to show that each distinguishable variety of sensation or state has one condition (or set of conditions) which always produces it; yet this ideal is often unattainable and hypotheses proposing it must be tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a guiding aim for simplifying explanations, but treat claims of unique antecedents as hypotheses subject to verification and open to discovery of further links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explanatory success where phenomenon is same in quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific explanation is most successful where the phenomenon is the same in quality across instances (motion is cited as especially amenable to unification because it is always of the same kind, differing only in degree or direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target unifying laws in domains where the sensed phenomenon doesn't change in kind (e.g., mechanics, wave propagation). Expect greater difficulty where phenomenological kinds differ.
